query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, the high‐temperature BCC phase is maintained by sluggish diffusion of Al (and its resulting pairwise interactions with the other elements) that kinetically suppresses the thermodynamic drive toward phase separation. Only when the system is held at lower temperatures for extended periods does atomic mobility permit transformation into secondary phases.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy in a single-phase high-temperature BCC state.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled annealing at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 600–800°C) with varied hold times versus rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted in an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, with identical starting compositions and microstructures, comparing extended isothermal holds (allowing moderate diffusion) against rapid cooling that preserves the metastable BCC phase.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic pairwise interactions—especially the effect of Al causing lattice distortions and lowering atomic mobility—which control nucleation barriers for secondary phases.
generation.mechanism: Although thermodynamics slightly favor the formation of secondary phases (e.g., L12 or sigma structures) at lower temperatures, the high activation energy for Al diffusion (and possibly coupled interactions with Cr, Co, Fe, and Ni) kinetically delays the transformation. Thus, the BCC phase persists unless sufficient thermal energy and time allow diffusion-driven rearrangement.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under prolonged annealing at 600–800°C, the high-temperature BCC phase will gradually decompose into secondary phases indicative of thermodynamic equilibration, while rapid cooling maintains the single-phase BCC state.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy exhibits a uniform high-temperature BCC structure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold within the temperature regime where atomic diffusion (particularly for Al) is moderately activated but not overwhelmingly so (i.e., below the original BCC stability threshold and away from temperatures causing complete melting or entirely different phase formations). Extremely high temperatures or non-thermal mechanical interventions may override the kinetic limitation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contributions of the thermodynamic driving force versus the kinetic barrier (e.g., precise activation energies of Al diffusion and interaction energies) have not been fully determined. Minor compositional fluctuations or processing variations could also modulate the balance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several specimens of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in the high-temperature BCC state. Subject one set to rapid quenching (baseline) and other sets to isothermal annealing at 600–800°C for different durations. Use X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and atom probe tomography to monitor the appearance and growth of secondary phases.
measurements: XRD patterns to detect new peaks associated with secondary phases
TEM imaging to observe morphology and distribution of precipitates
Atom probe tomography to assess changes in elemental distributions (particularly Al)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If extended annealing at these temperatures does not result in a statistically significant emergence of secondary phases (i.e., the microstructure and phase composition remain equivalent to the rapidly quenched control), then the hypothesis that kinetic suppression of atomic mobility is governing phase stability in the alloy would be falsified.

## Abstract
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are of particular interest due to their unique combination of high strength, ductility, and fracture resistance. These properties are largely impacted by the phases and number of phases present in the alloy. Due to the enormous chemical design space, with typically five or six elements present in the alloys in addition to the various processing parameters, the prediction of the number of phases is challenging. While there have been multiple recent reports of phase predictions through data-driven models, an alternate approach is proposed and demonstrated here. In this work, phase prediction is performed using features derived from DFT-calculated pairwise interactions among constituent elements (incorporating bonding and structure) rather than relying solely on traditional elemental descriptors such as electronegativity. By focusing on atomic interaction features, our model provides a novel perspective on the phase stability in HEAs. This approach yields a predictive model for phase formation in HEAs that is comparable in accuracy to prior models while offering improved interpretability. These alloys have been extensively studied due to their favorable mechanical properties. For instance, the ultimate tensile strength can reach up to 700 MPa, which is comparable to austenitic stainless steels. −  The tensile ductility for most 3d transition HEAs falls in the range of 40–60%.
